title: test-0063-SOC-HIS-COUNTRYSIDE
passage: Many people mistakenly believe that the Permanent Settlement made zamindars the absolute, permanent owners of their land, but this is incorrect. Under this system, if a zamindar failed to pay the fixed revenue to the British on time, their land was auctioned off, meaning their rights were conditional, not absolute. Furthermore, some students assume that indigo was a chemical dye produced in factories, but it was actually a natural plant-based dye extracted from the indigo shrub. The cultivation of this plant was highly problematic for farmers. Planters often forced peasants to grow indigo on their best land, which exhausted the soil's fertility so quickly that rice could not be grown there afterwards. Additionally, the cash advances provided by planters were not meant to make peasants rich; instead, they trapped farmers in a cycle of debt. While some believe the Blue Rebellion was a conflict between two groups of Indian farmers, it was actually a massive uprising by the ryots against the oppressive British planters. Finally, it is a common myth that indigo protests only began with Mahatma Gandhi in 1917, yet the major Blue Rebellion occurred much earlier, in 1859, when thousands of ryots refused to grow indigo and attacked the factories.
summary: Planters often forced peasants to grow indigo on their best land, which made the soil dry quickly, so rice couldn't grow there.
